Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands

IX. The Earlier Philosophers’ View: The Soul Understands by Joining the Active Intellect
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00907

The standard view in many books by philosophers of the Islamic period is that this account, like the one just discussed, is false. The two views are closely related. Their argument is that the Active Intellect must either be one simple being or a composite made of parts. If it is one simple being, then a soul that joins with it in order to understand one thing would join with it in order to understand every intelligible thing. If the soul joins with only one part of it, not the whole, then the Active Intellect must have a part for every act of understanding a human being can achieve. But human beings can understand endlessly many things, so it would have endlessly many parts of different kinds. Each of these intelligible things could be understood by endlessly many souls. Zayd's understanding of blackness, for example, would be like Amr's understanding of blackness. The Active Intellect would therefore need endlessly many parts of the same kind, repeated endlessly many times.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00908

That is already impossible. There is another problem: parts of the same kind could differ only by their essence or by features that follow from their essence, or else by changeable accidents. But changeable accidents require matter. The Active Intellect is free of matter, so its parts would be even less likely to differ by accidents. They would not be distinct, and so it could not have many parts. It would have to be simple, contrary to the assumption that it is composite. This is the argument later thinkers repeat when they reject this view. Avicenna points to it in The Pointers: those who hold the view must either divide the Active Intellect so that one part joins the soul at a time, or say that the soul joins it in one act and thereby becomes complete and able to understand everything.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00909

I say that this view, like the one before it, was held by distinguished earlier philosophers. It must have a subtle and sound meaning, even if it takes careful thought, a clear mind, and God's help to uncover it. We pleaded with Him through our minds, raising our inward hands to Him, not only our passing bodily hands. We laid ourselves before Him and begged Him to reveal this question and others like it, with the persistence of someone driven to seek help and unwilling to give up. Then He lit our minds with His radiant light and lifted some of the veils and obstacles. We have seen the intellectual world as one being, joined to all the beings in our world. They begin from it and return to it. It is the source of intelligible things and all essences, yet it does not divide into parts, lose anything as things flow from it, or gain anything when things join it. The proof of this reality belongs elsewhere in the book. Here I will give three points that may ease people's doubts about the soul joining that world whenever it understands something.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00910

First, as we have already proved, when the soul understands something, it becomes that intellectual form. Second, the intellect is all intelligible things. We have proved this elsewhere. This does not mean that all things come together in one place with all their separate bodily existences. A horse has an outside existence with size, position, color, and matter. It also has a distinct intellectual existence with intellectual features that belong to that mode of being. Just as individual horses exist in the senses and occupy different places, each kind also has its own intellectual existence. In that mode, the understood horse is one thing and the understood plant another.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00911

Rather, all the essences that exist outside the mind as many separate things can exist in the intellect in one intellectual existence that gathers their meanings while remaining simple and one. Third, the unity of intellects is not numerical unity, like the unity of bodies, blackness, color, or motion. If two bodies of the same size existed, they would be larger together than either one alone. Two black things likewise make more blackness than either by itself. Intellectual unity works differently. If we imagined a thousand intellects like one intellect, the unity of each would be no greater or less than the unity of the thousand together.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00912

Consider the idea of a human being in general. If you added another idea just like it, leaving aside differences of position, size, place, and other accidents, you would not find anything different in the second idea or in the pair that was not already present in the first. The author of The Book of Lights says: “Pure existence, which has no greater degree, remains itself when you suppose it a second time, because nothing can distinguish pure existence.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00913

With these points clear, we can say that the human soul can understand all realities and become one with them. It can also become an intellectual world containing the form of every intellectual being and the meaning of every bodily being. Suppose, for example, that the intellectual meaning of a horse is present in the soul. We have established that one intellectual meaning, with one definition and kind but no individual features or location, cannot be multiplied in existence unless something is added to its meaning. So the intellectual horse in the Active Intellect and the intellectual horse in a soul that has become intellect in act cannot differ in meaning or essence. They are one and the same meaning; any difference between them must come from something beyond their definition.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00914

We have also shown that the soul becomes one with every intellectual form it understands. It follows that, in that respect, it joins with the Active Intellect, which contains all things. It does not join with what it has not understood. Since all the meanings exist there in one existence without multiplying or dividing it, their appearing as many things in other places does not divide the Active Intellect. In the same way, many souls can join with it through their different perfections without dividing it, and without every soul receiving every perfection. Anyone who finds this difficult is treating intellectual unity as if it were numerical unity.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00915

For example, a human being is one with the universal meaning “animal,” and so are a horse, an ox, and a lion. Yet they do not become one another. “Animal” is a universal meaning that can be one with different kinds. The intellectual world can likewise hold many meanings together. The First Teacher says in The Theology of Aristotle that the higher world is the complete living being that contains all things. It came from the first, perfect Creator and contains every soul and every intellect. Nothing there is poor or needy. Everything there is full of life and richness, as if life were flowing from one spring—not like one single heat or wind, but like one quality that contains every quality and every taste.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00916

He says further that the different kinds of life and intellect in our world come from different movements of life and intellect. That is why there are different animals and intellects, some brighter and nobler than others. Some intellects are close to the first intellects and so shine more brightly; others are second or third in rank. Here, some are divine, some rational, and some nonrational, because they are farther from the noble intellects. But in the higher world, all things have intellect. So a horse is intellect, and the intellect of a horse is a horse. The intellect that understands a horse is not the intellect that understands a human being; that would be impossible for the first intellects.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00917

When the First Intellect understands something, it and what it understands are one. It does not understand anything that has no intellect; it understands it through its universal intellect and universal life. Individual life does not lack universal life, and likewise an individual intellect does not lack universal intellect. The intellect in an animal is not cut off from the First Intellect. Each part of intellect contains all that can be divided from it. The intellect of a thing is potentially all the things it can understand; when it becomes actual, it is particular and complete. When it is fully actual, it is a horse or some other animal. As life descends to lower forms, it becomes weaker and less complete. Some of its powers become hidden, and weaker animals appear. When their life is weak, intellect compensates by giving them strong body parts: some have claws, some horns, and some fangs. That is the end of the First Teacher's words.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00918

These words clarify and support what I have argued, though some of them need explanation so that readers do not misunderstand them. When he speaks of different “movements” of life and intellect, he means different intellectual aspects in the first intellects, such as necessity and possibility, greater and lesser strength, and the differences that come from being nearer to or farther from the first Creator. “Movement” here means a source or outflow, not change. Differences in movement can be differences in kind, such as whether something flows from the aspect of necessity and existence or from the aspect of essence and possibility. They can also be differences in degree, depending on nearness to or distance from the First. What flows from a higher intellect close to the First is nobler than what flows from a lower one.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00919

When he says that some intellects are close to the first intellects, he means the intellects that exist apart from matter in act. By the “second” and “third,” he means the essences of kinds and their intellectual forms, which have different levels. The first are human intellects, the second animal, and the third plant. When he says that something cannot be understood by the first intellects, he means the intellects in the lower ranks. When he says that individual life does not lack universal life, by “universal life” he means the nature of animal, and by “universal intellect” its universal intellectual form.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00920

Each of these, depending on how we consider it, differs from the first actual intellect, while still being one with it in existence. An essence considered in itself can be universal or particular, separate from matter or embodied, and so on. Its intellectual form, however, is shared in act by all its actual or possible individuals. The first actual intellect is the existence and intellectual identity that gathers many particular meanings.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00921

When he says that the intellect in an animal is not cut off from the First Intellect, he means that the animal's intellectual nature is not cut off from it, because that nature is one with it. When he speaks of parts of intellect, he means meaningful parts that can be intellectual forms of bodily parts: the understood head, hand, and foot of an understood animal. Each one has the same kinds of existence as the whole, such as being understood or sensed. And when he says that the intellect of a thing is potentially all things, he uses “potential” and “actual” in a special sense, not the usual one. “Potential” means that one existence, in its unity, gathers many essences and meanings that may appear as many existences elsewhere. As when strong blackness is said to be all weaker blackness potentially, he does not mean it can be divided into them or is ready to be affected by them. It is a pure existence, fully actual and without any lack. “Actual” here means that a bodily thing is brought into being with material qualities. The rest of his words are clear once these ideas are understood.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00922
X. Refuting a Later View of Knowledge
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00923

One later thinker says that knowledge and awareness are relations, and that a relation exists only when both things it connects exist. If what is understood is the knower itself, he says, then that knower cannot exist without understanding itself. No further image needs to be formed in it; its being a knower is simply its relation to itself as the understood thing. But if the understood thing differs from the knower, the knower cannot understand it while it is absent from the outside world. So an image of that thing must be formed in the knower to create the relation called understanding. This is the rule, he says, that the arguments support. Since an image must be present and knowledge cannot simply be the image itself, a further relation must be added to it. Once all other possibilities have been ruled out, this must be the correct account.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00924

This view and the argument supporting it are very weak. We have already shown by clear proof that knowledge is a form of existence free of matter. Anyone who looks inward will see that knowledge, like power, is a perfection of a living being. A bare relation is not a perfection in itself. The argument is weak too, because it never tells us what kind of relation knowledge is. Relation is itself a broad category, and it needs further features to become one specific kind. The same argument could be used for nearly every relation-based feature, such as power, will, desire, anger, love, fear, pain, and mercy. We could say that willing is a relation that exists only when both sides exist.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00925

If the one who wills is also what is willed, then it cannot fail to will itself while it exists. No further image needs to be formed; its being a willer is simply its relation to itself as the willed thing. But if what is willed differs from the willer, and is absent from the outside world, then an image must be present in or before the willer for the relation of willing to exist. The same argument would apply to power and to every other such feature.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00926

If someone replies that one thing cannot be both able and subject to power, or that it cannot move itself or be angry with itself, we answer that these facts are not contained in the concept of power alone. To know that the one who has power differs from what it acts on, or that the mover differs from what is moved, we need an argument beyond the meanings of those words. The same is true of father and child, or an angry person and the one they are angry with. Avicenna explains this point in several places in The Healing. We will return to it and explain it further.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00927
XI. How One Thing Can Be Intellect, Knower, and Known Without Becoming Many
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00928

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī says that literal-minded people admired this grand, poetic claim and concluded that a knower must become one with what it understands, whether it understands itself or something else. But careful thinkers, he says, rejected union and instead claimed that when a thing understands itself, the intellect, the knower, and the intelligible are one.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00929

I thank God, who showed us this path. With His help and light, we have made clear what many philosophers, let alone other scholars, could not see. No one should still doubt it unless they misunderstand the argument or cannot follow it. There is no disagreement among philosophers that an immaterial substance understands itself and is understood by itself, without becoming many things or needing an extra feature beyond its existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00930

In the eighth part of The Healing, Avicenna says that God is complete, indeed beyond complete, and is pure intellect because being in matter and tied to matter prevents something from being understood and from being an intellect. What is free of matter and exists apart from it is understood by itself. Since it is an intellect in itself, it is also understood in itself. So it is intellect, knower, and intelligible—not three separate things. As a separate identity, it is an intellect. Considered as an identity that is separate for itself, it is intelligible to itself. And considered as an identity that belongs to itself, it is the knower of itself. The knower is something whose nature is separate for something; the intelligible is something whose nature is separate for something. That “something” need not be another thing; it can be the same thing or another. The concept of knower requires an intelligible, but it does not say whether that intelligible is the same thing or something else. The same is true of motion and what causes motion: the concept alone does not tell us whether the mover and what is moved are one or two. We need a separate argument to show that something cannot move itself. The meanings of relations likewise do not by themselves tell us whether their two sides are distinct.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00931

Al-Rāzī objects that the thing understood and the knower may be the same, but the descriptions “knower” and “intelligible” are not the same. He says that we can judge something to be understood without judging that it understands, and we can judge that it understands without judging that it is understood. So they must be two distinct positive features. Someone may reply that we cannot understand a thing as a knower without also understanding it as intelligible, and vice versa; this would show that they are one. Al-Rāzī answers that each description has its own meaning. If one referred to the other, whenever we grasped one we would grasp the other, just as “human being” and “person” name one nature. But we can grasp the meaning of knower without grasping the meaning of intelligible, and vice versa. So the two features differ. And if two features differ in one case, he says, they differ in every case. Blackness differs in nature from motion wherever either is found.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00932

We answer that the two descriptions are tied together, but that does not make what is described one and the same meaning. Knowing that someone is a parent goes with knowing that someone is a child, yet parenthood and childhood are different. If something is moving, knowing it is moving goes with knowing there is something that moves it; but “moving” and “mover” do not mean the same thing. So the knower and the intelligible differ in meaning, while the same being can have both descriptions. That it is intellect is an even clearer case of a different meaning from its being a knower or intelligible. That is the end of al-Rāzī's argument.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00933

This scholar has spent much time on argument but has not understood the difference between a thing's meaning and its existence. He assumes that if two meanings differ, then their existences must differ too. But God's essential perfections—knowledge, power, will, life, hearing, and sight—are one being and one existence. His necessity, existence, and unity are also one reality, with no difference in His being, whether we consider Him in the mind, outside it, or by analysis.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00934

The essential features of a thing may have many meanings, while still existing in one way, especially in a simple being. So a difference between meanings in one place does not prove a difference in existence elsewhere. If positive attributes differed in existence, the being described by them would be many and composite. That would make the one divine being composite. Al-Rāzī's view also erases the difference between being a knower and being intelligible, on the one hand, and being a parent and a child, on the other. If one thing can be both knower of itself and intelligible to itself, with the two features different in both meaning and existence, then why could it not also be its own parent and child, or move itself? The philosophers agree that one thing cannot move itself, be its own parent, or teach itself. Yet they accept that one thing can understand itself and be understood by itself. Some accomplished mystics even say that the simple intellect is all intelligible things. This shows that meanings can differ without their existence differing. One simple being, from one simple side, can be the true source for many meanings without losing its unity.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00935

When philosophers say that two features differ in their basis or point of view, as movement and being moved, potentiality and actuality, possibility and necessity, or unity and multiplicity, they do not infer this from the meanings alone. There must be something else, as Avicenna himself says in the passage we quoted. Al-Rāzī also argues that we know for certain that we have a power by which we understand things. Is the power by which we understand that power the same power, so that it understands itself? Or is it another power? If it is another, then we have one power for understanding things and another for understanding that power, and so on without end. This would mean we have an actual infinite number of powers. So the fact that something is understood does not require a different thing to understand it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00936

Avicenna also says in The Annotations that God's understanding Himself and being understood by Himself do not make Him two in His being or in how we consider Him. His being is one, and our way of considering Him is one. The words put the ideas in a different order, but the point is the same.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00937

It is now clear that a form free of matter can, by its very existence and without any added feature, be intellect, knower, and intelligible. These meanings all exist in one being. They are not simply different words that mean the same thing, as some people think philosophers say about God's attributes. Nor is it right to object, as al-Rāzī does, that philosophers cannot say God's existence is the same as His being because existence is easy to understand while God's essence is unknowable. The same objection applies to His other attributes, whose meanings are familiar even though His essence is not fully known. This objection assumes that philosophers claim the meanings are identical in concept, as if they were synonyms. They mean instead that the meanings are one in existence, as when a subject is said to have different features in ordinary predication.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00938

Al-Rāzī then says that understanding must be a relation, because he has proved that it is relational. A relation, he says, must differ from the thing itself. The philosophers think that understanding is just presence, and that another image of the thing cannot be present to itself. So they claim that the thing's own existence is its understanding. But since, as he argues, understanding is relational, it must be a feature separate from the knower. He offers this proof: if knowing something were the same as the thing's own being, then the reality of knowing and the reality of the thing would be identical, and one could not exist without the other. Yet we can understand a thing without understanding that it understands itself, and we can understand that it is a knower without understanding what it understands. So knowing itself must be something added to the thing. This added feature cannot be an image that matches the thing, for a familiar proof rules out two identical things together. So it must be something different. If this different feature is related to the thing, the thing is known through that relation. If it is not related to the thing and does not match it in nature, then the thing's reality is neither present nor related to the mind, and it cannot be known. Therefore, he concludes, knowledge is a relation.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00939

I am surprised that this scholar, whom people call “the Imam,” has made such a mistake about knowledge. The very thing that perfects every living being, gives every excellent being its excellence, and lights the way to our beginning and return, is treated by him as one of the weakest and most dependent accidents. Did he not consider the words of God about the blessed: “Their light will run before them and to their right”? Did he not reflect on “Whoever God does not give light to has no light,” or on “Are those who know equal to those who do not know?” Did he not consider the Prophet's saying, “Faith is a light that God casts into the heart of the believer”? How could this and similar things be only a relation, which exists in neither the outside world nor the mind apart from the two things it connects?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00940

The foundation of his argument is again the failure to distinguish a thing's meaning from its existence. We have often explained that one essence can have several kinds of existence, each different in its being. Many essences with different meanings can also have one simple existence, in reality and in how it is considered.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00941

When al-Rāzī says that if knowing oneself is one's very being, then whatever is true of the being must be true of the knowing, and vice versa, we answer: if “reality” means existence, these two statements work in both directions and cause no problem. It is true to say that whenever the separate substance exists, its awareness of itself exists; and whenever its awareness of itself exists, that very awareness is the separate substance. If he means that the two meanings or essences are identical, then his conclusion does not follow. No philosopher claims that the concept of knowing is the same as the concept of an immaterial being. His mistake comes from mixing up meaning with existence, or essence with individual reality.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00942

Someone who says knowledge is only a relation should ask what gives rise to that relation and why it belongs to some things, not others, and connects some things rather than others. In truth, every relation that exists requires some settled, positive existence in one or both of its sides before the relation can arise. That existence is the source of the relation. It may be the very being of one side, or a feature added to it. A relation can never stand on its own.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00943
XII. Further Questions About Self-Knowledge
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00944

It has been asked: whether we say that perception is a relation, or that it is the perceived form appearing in the one who perceives it, how can a thing know itself? If knowledge is a relation, then a relation must hold between two things. One thing cannot be related to itself, so it cannot know itself. And if knowledge is the appearance of a form, a thing’s form appears to something else. It makes no sense to say that it appears to itself.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00945

The truth, as we have already explained, is that knowledge is a thing’s actual existence for something. More precisely, knowledge is the existence of something immaterial, whether that existence is for itself or for something else. If it exists for another, it is that other thing’s knowledge; if it does not exist for another, it is knowledge of itself.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00946

Existence works in the same way. A thing may exist for itself, as substances do, or for something else, as accidents exist for the things in which they occur. But the relation between existence and essence is only a way of speaking, since they differ only when the mind analyzes them. A relation distinguishes its two sides within the setting where the relation holds, not necessarily in every other setting. If the relation exists in the outside world—as with father and child, or writer and what is written—it requires the two sides to be distinct in that world. One person cannot be both the father and the child in the same relation. But when a relation exists only in the mind, the two sides differ only within that relation and in the way the mind considers them. This second kind has two forms.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00947

In the first, the two sides are one in outside existence but have different essences. The difference between them is enough for one to have a feature or role in thought that the other does not. Essence and existence are like this. Though they are one in reality, the mind considers one as something that receives existence and the other as the existence it receives. The relation between them makes them distinct within that analysis, not in the outside world, where there is no such division.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00948

In the second form, the two sides do not differ at all, either outside the mind or in its analysis. This is possible only in something utterly simple, with no composition of any kind, such as God. When we call Him self-existing, self-sustaining, self-knowing, powerful, willing, or living, there is in reality no relation, attribute, connection, or subject bearing an added feature. There is only pure existence, which itself is the reality meant by knowledge, power, will, life, and every other perfection.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00949

The mind speaks of a subject, an attribute, and a relation because it has seen these features occur in created things. In some things, such features are added to what bears them, and that gives rise to a real relation between them. But the proof that none of existence and its perfections is added to God means that His existence, knowledge, power, will, and other attributes all rest in His own being. This relation between God and Himself is something the mind considers by analogy with created things, to show that no additions belong to Him—not to establish a real relation within God. The relation is figurative: it means that composition and multiplicity are absent from Him. The difference between the two sides is figurative too. The relation of the simple, immaterial self to its own knowledge belongs to this same kind. It does not create multiplicity outside or inside the mind, because the relation itself is only something the mind considers. In our account, knowledge is immaterial existence. Just as existence exists for itself, it is also intelligible to itself. Neither self-existence nor self-understanding makes the one simple reality two things or gives it two separate aspects. The difference lies only in the meanings we use.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00950

As we have seen, different meanings can belong to one and the same reality. One simple existence, with no trace of composition, can be what many meanings refer to, even though those same meanings may belong to different things elsewhere. An immaterial being, because it is not in a subject, is called a substance. Because it is a form free of matter, it is called an intellect. Because it is a form of itself, it is called intelligible. Because it exists for itself rather than for another, it is called a knower. Because it is existence free of evil and therefore lovable, and because it perceives that goodness, it loves itself. In this way, many relational meanings can apply to one reality without making it multiple or different in itself; the multiplicity is in the meanings.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00951

Let us return to some objections. The critic says that, according to Avicenna, for a thing to be understood means that its immaterial essence is present to something. This is broader in meaning than saying that its essence is present to something other than itself. Someone might object that this is exactly the problem: being present to something is a relation, and a relation can hold only between two things. If a thing can be said to move itself because “moving” is broader than “moving something else,” why not also say that a thing can create itself because “creating” is broader than “creating something else”?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00952

The answer is that neither self-understanding nor self-motion is proved merely by saying that one meaning is broader than another. Each needs a separate argument. The philosopher is not claiming that the broader meaning alone proves that a thing can understand itself. That would be like arguing that since something can be an animal, it can therefore be human. The broader meaning does not prove the narrower one, though it does not rule it out either.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00953

Avicenna’s point is to remove a supposed contradiction. Someone might think that “a thing knows” necessarily means that the known thing differs from the knower, as with other relations, and so cannot be identical with it even in meaning. Avicenna points out that the concept of a relation itself requires only a difference in meaning between the related sides. It does not, by itself, show that they must differ in existence. In some relations, outside proof establishes that the two sides must be different in existence. For example, “mover” means something that begins a gradual change, but the concept itself does not tell us whether the mover is different from what it moves. We know by other arguments that a mover, creator, or agent must differ in existence and identity from what is moved, created, or acted upon. A thing’s perceiving or existing for itself, by contrast, involves a difference in meaning while knower and known, or existent and existence, are one in identity and existence, as the proof has shown. Likewise, we know by argument, not merely from the concepts, that a thing cannot be both cause and effect of itself. This is how we should understand the following words from one of the scholars:
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00954

Knowledge is among relational things. If one and the same being is considered under two descriptions, it is as though we were considering two beings. What belongs to it as knower differs from what belongs to it as known. The one being can therefore bear the relation in view of these two distinct aspects.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00955

It is also reported that Avicenna wrote in The Discussions that each individual has an essence and an individuality, and that individuality is always additional to essence. If the essence itself determines that individuality, then the kind exists in only that individual; otherwise, there will be many individuals of that kind. The essence, he says, differs from the whole made up of that essence and its individuality. This difference is enough for the essence to be related as knower to the whole, and for the whole to be related as known to the essence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00956

I have not seen a copy of The Discussions, and this passage does not sound like Avicenna. For knowing and being known in themselves are features of existence, not of essence considered by itself. Individuation is not something added to existence. A thing’s existence comes before its essence and before any relation between its essence and existence. So if an essence is related to an individual that exists only after that essence exists, the essence can be related to that individual only after it has itself become individual. The thing that is related to itself would then be the individual, and the relation would belong to one individual in one and the same respect. The earlier account is better.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00957

Someone might object that individuation is an existent feature, and so its existence must come after the existence of the thing it individuates. We reply that the same issue arises with a defining feature in relation to the broader kind it completes, existence in relation to the essence it makes actual, and form in relation to the matter it completes. As we explained earlier, things are described by such features within the mind’s analysis, not as separate features in existence. In reality, they are one with the things they describe.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00958
XIII. Kinds of Perception
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00959

We perceive things in four ways: through our senses, through imagination, through our grasp of meanings tied to particular things, and through reason. Sensation perceives a thing that exists in matter and is present to the perceiver, together with its particular sensible features: where and when it is, its position, quality, quantity, and other features. Some of these features always belong to the thing in the outside world, while others may vary; but what is directly sensed and present to the perceiver is the thing’s form, not the material thing itself. Before a sensible thing makes an impression on the sense, the sense is no more actually sensing than it was before. Once the impression occurs, it must fit the nature of the sense. Otherwise, it would not be an act of sensing that thing. So the sense receives the thing’s form, separated from its matter, though it does not separate the form completely.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00960

Imagination perceives the same thing with those features, whether its matter is present or absent. Imagination can picture only what has first been sensed. The third kind, often called estimation, grasps a meaning the senses do not directly perceive. It does not grasp that meaning as universal, but as belonging to a particular sensed thing. That tie to one particular thing makes the meaning particular. Understanding through reason grasps a thing in terms of what it is, whether considered on its own or together with other features that can also be understood in this way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00961

Every act of perception involves some degree of separation. Sensation requires three conditions: the matter must be present to the sense, the thing must be surrounded by particular features, and the thing perceived must be an individual. Imagination is free of the first condition, estimation of the first two, and understanding through reason of all three. Know, however, that the difference between this third kind and understanding through reason does not lie in the act of perceiving itself. It lies in something added to it: whether or not what is perceived is tied to a particular individual. In reality, then, there are three kinds of perception, just as there are three worlds. Estimation is like an intellect that has fallen from its proper level. Every act of perception draws the realities and spirits of things out of the forms of bodies and structures of matter. The sensible form is drawn out only partly, and remains tied to the presence of matter. The imagined form is drawn out to a middle degree, which is why imagination belongs to a world between the worlds of sense and intellect. The intellectual form is drawn out completely.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00962

This is how it works when forms are taken from matter. But something that is itself an intellect needs no such separation in order to be understood. These are the meanings through which the soul is meant to become an ordered intellectual world: from the First Principle, through the intellects who are the angels nearest to God, then the souls that are angels below them, and on through the heavens, the elements, the forms of the whole, and its nature. The soul thus becomes a bright intellectual world, lit by the First Intellect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00963

Likewise, something that is itself an imaginal form needs no separation in order to be imagined. When the soul connects with such a form, it becomes a world of the hereafter, a vast realm as wide as the heavens and the earth. The worlds are what they are through their forms, not through their matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00964

The incidental features from which we must separate a thing in order to understand it are not its essence or meaning. There is no conflict between understanding one thing and also understanding another feature alongside it. The same is true of imagination: the features that must be set aside are not other imaginal forms, since one thing can be imagined together with another. What blocks some kinds of perception is instead a mode of existence that is dark and bound up with absences, concealing things from perception. Existence in matter, with its position and dimensions, can hide a form from perception altogether.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00965

Being in sensation or imagination can also block intellectual perception, because both are dimensional forms of existence, even when they are free of matter. An intelligible does not exist in a dimensional way. It is free of both modes and beyond both worlds. The different modes of existence therefore occupy different levels: some are intellectual, some belong to the soul, and some are dark and beyond perception. Essences follow each level of existence. A human being, for example, can exist as a particular material person, as a human soul, or as a universal intellectual reality that contains all people in one collective unity, without multiplying into separate human beings.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00966

This resolves a familiar problem. A universal intellectual form exists in an individual soul as an attribute exists in the thing it belongs to. Its being in that soul, its particularity, and its relation to the soul’s other features are all particular features that cannot be separated from it. How, then, can the intellect abstract a form from such incidental features?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00967

A common answer is that the shared human nature found in individuals is, in itself, free of such features. Knowledge of it is called universal because its object is universal, not because the act of knowing is universal in itself. Later thinkers misunderstood this explanation. They assumed it meant that the intellect contains a universal form, then rejected the answer by saying that the humanity in Zayd is not the same as the humanity in ʿAmr. The shared humanity that applies to both is not identical with the humanity in either one individually, nor is it a thing that exists in both at once. If it existed in one person, it would be only part of a supposed whole made up of both persons; and the same would apply to three or more individuals. In the outside world, the number of instances of humanity matches the number of individuals.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00968

Still, if we consider the essence of a human without adding any condition, it is simply what it is: neither one nor many, neither universal nor particular. In that respect, it is compatible with each of these descriptions. With an individual, it is particular; with a universal, it is universal; with one, it is one; with many, it is many. The universal humanity shared by many individuals exists only in the intellect. As one form in one intellect, such as Zayd’s intellect, it is an individual form. As it relates to each of the individuals, it is universal. To say that it relates to them means that the nature grasped by this form could occur in many people: if it were present in the matter of any one of them, it would yield that very person; and whichever person an intelligent observer first encountered, the same form could be grasped from them. This is what it means for the form to be shared.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00969

Its abstraction means that this nature has been drawn from the external material features of individuals, even though, in another respect, it is surrounded by mental features that make it particular. In one respect, it is used to understand something else; in another, it is itself what the mind considers. We, however, see no conflict between an intellectual form being particular in its own mode of existence and being universal or shared among many. As we have explained, an intellectual form does not inhere in the mind the way an accident inheres in its subject, becoming particular through the mind’s own particularity or the features surrounding the soul.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00970

As long as the soul is confined to these psychic conditions, it cannot become an intellect in act, and its object of thought cannot become intelligible in act. While the soul exists in its natural or psychic mode, it has only the potential to be intellect and intelligible. When it sheds that mode and enters a new one, its existence and individuality become intellectual and universal. It can then become one with the objects of thought, and its relation to individual people is equal. In short, an intellectual form is not surrounded by psychic features, nor does it exist in the psychic way of such states as desire, anger, fear, grief, or courage. We have also explained that abstraction in understanding and other forms of perception does not mean removing incidental features one by one. Nor does it mean that the soul stays still while the perceived things move from matter to the senses, then from the senses to imagination, and from imagination to intellect. The perceiver and what it perceives are abstracted together. They pass together from one mode of existence to another, from one level of being to another, until the soul becomes intellect, knower, and intelligible in act, after being all three only in possibility.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00971
XIV. How the Rational Power Unifies Many Things and Distinguishes One Thing into Many
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00972

In our account, the intellect unifies many things by becoming an intellectual world, one with every reality and the source of every intelligible meaning. It is a simple intellect that gives rise to the soul’s many distinct acts of knowledge. Most philosophers explain this in two other ways. First, by analysis: if we strip away the individual features and other accidents from people who fall under one species, the one shared nature remains. Second, by combination: the intellect can join a defining feature to a broader kind, so that together they form one unified essence, either as a real unity or as a unity in predication.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00973

The intellect can also distinguish one thing into many. It does so by giving intellectual realities bodily shape through imagination and placing them in imaginal forms. It is also said to do so by distinguishing what belongs to a thing in itself from what is accidental to it; a thing’s broader kind from the feature that distinguishes it; its kind from higher kinds in the chain; one distinguishing feature from another; and what is inseparable from it from what can be separated, as well as what is near to it from what is far away. Thus one thing to the senses can be many things to the intellect.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00974

That is why intellectual perception is the fullest kind of perception. The intellect does not stop at a thing’s surface or outward form. It enters into the thing’s essence and reality and forms a matching image of it in every respect. Indeed, it becomes that reality in its essence. Sense perception, by contrast, is mixed with ignorance and reaches its object only partly. The senses grasp the outer forms and appearances of things, not their inner realities.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00975
XV. Levels of the Intellect and What It Understands
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00976

The philosophers say that there are three kinds of understanding. The first is the intellect in potentiality: it is not yet any of the intelligible forms, nor does it actually contain any of them. But the soul can acquire all intelligible forms and rise through their levels. The potential intellect is a world of intellect in possibility, capable of perceiving all realities and receiving the forms of every existent that is intelligible in itself because it is free of matter. For things that are not intelligible in themselves—because they are forms in matter, sense, or imagination—the rational power can separate their forms from matter, as the philosophers have explained and as we will explain, God willing. The soul then becomes able to produce and receive distinct intellectual forms. The world of forms has two sides: an intellectual world and a sensory world. A sensory world is what it is through its form, not its matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00977

When a thing’s form is present in something as it truly is, that thing itself becomes a world. The potential intellect is ready to become a world containing all things, once it receives the forms of both worlds. Through the forms it understands, it resembles the intellectual world; through its own form, it resembles the sensory world. In its own being, it can contain the essence and form of every existent.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00978

If it cannot grasp something, that may be because the thing has a weak, non-formal kind of existence, close to nonexistence. This includes prime matter, motion, time, potentiality, and the infinite. Or it may be because the thing’s existence is so intense and manifest that it overwhelms the soul’s own existence and light. This is the case with the First Principle and the highest intellects. The human soul’s existence in matter makes it too weak to grasp realities that are so luminous in themselves. Once it is freed from these attachments, it may turn toward them and know them fully. It can then become like the intellectual world, which is the form of all things in God’s knowledge, prior in reality to their existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00979

The potential intellect has many degrees, differing in strength and number. It may be close to actual understanding or far from it; it may be ready to grasp all things or only some. Each of these possibilities has countless degrees. At one extreme is someone deeply dull, with little power of understanding. At the other is someone exceptionally intelligent and naturally bright: the sacred power whose light is almost shining before the Active Intellect touches it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00980
The second kind is when the soul’s learned, detailed intellectual forms are present in the imaginative faculty, where it can observe them one by one.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00981

The third kind is a simple intellect: the intelligibles are present in it in act, not in potentiality, yet it is free of multiplicity and detail. Avicenna points to this simple intellect in the psychology section of The Healing. He says that there are three ways to understand. In the first, the intellect holds an idea in a clear, ordered, detailed form. In the second, the soul has learned an idea but has turned away from it and is attending to something else. We cannot hold many things in view all at once. The third is like what happens when someone is asked a question about something they have learned, or nearly learned, and the answer comes to mind at once. The person is sure of the answer before working out its details. As the person gives the answer, the details and their order unfold in the mind. This immediate certainty is the starting point of the later explanation.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00982

Someone might say that this, too, is knowledge only in potentiality, though close to becoming actual. Avicenna says that is wrong, because the person already has certainty in act and does not need to acquire it through a distant or nearby potential. That certainty must mean either that the person is sure the answer is there whenever they want to recall it, or that the answer is already certain in act. In the first case, the person is actually certain that the answer is present in them; in the second, the answer is certain in act as well. It is impossible to be sure that something presently unknown is stored in you. You cannot know the state of something without knowing it in some respect. Since your attention is directed to what is actually known, and you are certain that it is stored in you, then in this simple way it is already known to you; you are now about to make it known in another way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00983

There is something remarkable here. When this person begins teaching someone else, they unfold what they grasped all at once through the second kind of learning, arranging it step by step and alongside the words they speak. One of these is discursive knowledge; the other is simple knowledge. Simple knowledge does not consist of one image after another in the soul. Rather, it is one source from which images flow into the faculty that receives them. It is the active knowledge that gives rise to what we call discursive knowledge and is its source. This is the soul’s universal intellect, akin to the Active Intellect. The detailed forms belong to the soul insofar as it is a soul. If it had no detailed forms, it would have no knowledge belonging to the soul. How the rational soul can have a principle beyond itself, with a kind of knowledge different from the soul’s own, is a question you must examine within yourself.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00984

Pure intellect contains no multiplicity and no sequence of images. It is the source of every form that flows from it into the soul. We should understand separate beings in the same way: their knowledge of things is like this simple intellect. Their intellect does not receive forms, or exist as a picture of the forms in the world considered as soul. Every intellectual act of perception is a relation to forms free of matter and its accidents. The soul has this relation because it is a receptive substance shaped by those forms; intellect has it because it is an active, originating substance.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00985

In short, this is what Avicenna says. I reply that this simple intellect can be established only if we accept that the knower becomes one with what it understands, in the way we have proved. It is surprising that Avicenna accepted claims like the ones he makes here while strongly rejecting that union. If simple intellect exists in the human soul and in beings wholly separate from bodies and matter, and it contains intelligible meanings, how can it give souls forms that are not already present in it? How can it bring souls from potentiality to actuality through something it does not contain? And how can it store the forms of intelligibles that the soul has forgotten, while remaining simple?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00986

In the same chapter, Avicenna asks what happens to ideas that we learn and later forget. Do they remain fully present in the soul? If so, we would still understand them. Are they stored in the soul, the body, or one of the body’s powers? But bodily powers cannot hold forms grasped by the intellect. Or does each intellectual form exist on its own, with the intellect sometimes attending to it and sometimes turning away? That would be like a person’s reflection appearing in a mirror when the conditions are right. He rejects the first two options and says the last is correct. He also says he will show in the First Philosophy that such forms do not exist separately. This leaves simple intellect as the storehouse for intelligibles. But his account then faces the same question: how could the details of many forms be gathered in simple intellect without accepting that knower and known become one?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00987
This is one of the central questions of divine philosophy. It opens the way to a special understanding of divine unity, known through direct experience by those close to God.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00988

The question can be settled only by applying principles established earlier in this book: existence is fundamental, and essences are drawn from it; existence can grow stronger or weaker; and the stronger existence becomes, the more it gathers and contains universal meanings and intellectual essences. When existence reaches the level of a simple intellect, wholly free from bodies and dimensions, it becomes all intelligibles and all things in a way more complete and nobler than they are in their ordinary forms. Anyone who has not experienced this way of understanding cannot explain simple intellect, the source of detailed knowledge. That is why even many learned philosophers have found it hard to accept. Suhrawardī, for example, rejected it openly in The Discussions, The Pointers, and The Philosophy of Illumination, as did Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī and others like them.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00989

Suhrawardī says in The Discussions that the philosophers in Aristotle’s school explained God’s knowledge of Himself by saying that, since He knows Himself, He must also know what follows from His essence. His knowledge of those consequences is contained in His knowledge of Himself. When we understand humanity, for example, we also understand what follows from it. They then distinguish three cases: detailed knowledge already present; knowledge held in potentiality, ready to be recalled; and the case where someone is asked many questions at once and first grasps, in a single general act, that they can answer them all, then spells out each answer in detail. This general knowledge is one act of knowing many things, but it is not merely potential, because the person feels that it differs from the state before being asked. Suhrawardī says later thinkers found this explanation too loose and incomplete.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00990

He also writes that saying “knowledge of what follows from a thing is contained in knowledge of the thing itself” is imprecise. A critic could ask whether God knows Himself and what follows from Him together. If not, that is another problem and seems impossible. If He knows both, then since what follows from Him is not identical to Him, His knowledge of Himself differs from His knowledge of what follows. The two acts of knowledge would be separate. And because what follows depends on its source, knowledge of it must depend on knowledge of the source. As for the example of having many answers at once, the critic may deny that many questions are asked together: perhaps each is asked one by one, with an answer after each. Or perhaps before explaining the answer, the person has only a potential ability to give it, and the two kinds of potentiality differ only in degree.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00991

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī makes a similar argument in The Eastern Investigations. He says knowledge is either potential or actual and detailed. The third kind, simple knowledge, is impossible. If one simple intellectual image truly matched many different things, it would have to share their different essences, which is impossible. If, instead, simple understanding consisted of different images for different things, then detailed knowledge would already be present, since that is all detailed knowledge means. The account, he says, is therefore confused. Perhaps the philosophers mean only that the forms of many things arrive at once in simple knowledge, while detailed understanding receives them one by one over time. If so, he agrees, but this is no middle stage between pure potentiality and fully actual knowledge. It only means that several acts of knowledge may happen together or one after another.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00992

He adds that their view fails even if knowledge is only a relation: a relation to one thing is different from a relation to another, so many relations would amount to many separate acts of knowledge. A person who is certain they can answer a question knows only that they have the ability to give an answer that will meet it. They do not yet know the answer’s real nature. That nature remains unknown, though the fact that the answer will address the question is known. This is like knowing that the soul moves the body without knowing the soul’s true essence. So, he concludes, the philosophers’ account is false, and the proof given earlier shows that one act of knowledge cannot be knowledge of many things.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00993

I say that this question is too lofty and difficult for a thinker like this to reach its depth through reasoning and a store of familiar arguments. If it could be solved by discursive thought and following inherited opinions, Avicenna and those near his level would not have overlooked it. Yet Avicenna’s own writings show a contradiction: he affirms simple intellect while rejecting the union of knower and known.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00994
XVI. Whether the Soul Can Understand Many Things at Once
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00995

On the account we have established—that when the soul moves from potentiality to actuality it becomes a simple intellect that is all things—the matter is settled for us. Here is why. Knowledge and understanding are kinds of existence; existence is one with essence, and knowledge is one with what is known. Some kinds of existence are low and weak; others are noble and strong. The weak kind is like a thin outer shell, containing few meanings and fixed on one thing, such as a single quantity, however thick or extended it may be. A noble kind is like the inner core, able to contain many meanings, even if its dimensions are small or it has no dimensions at all, as with the rational soul.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00996

Knowledge also has many kinds. Some are weak, like sensation: one act of sense cannot perceive many different things. Others are noble, like intellection: one act of intellect can grasp countless intelligible things, as happens in simple intellect. In general, the higher knowledge is in existence, the more it contains what is known and the more it gathers essences into one. Knowledge belonging to the soul is between imagination and simple intellect. It can relate to two things at once, as when the mind judges that one thing belongs to another. To make that judgment, we must have both ideas present together: the subject and the predicate. Someone judging about two things must have both before the mind at that moment. Otherwise, only one idea would be present, and there could be no judgment. The judgment would then always have to contain several ideas. Likewise, if we know a thing by a complete definition, we know its whole essence. If we could not know all its parts together, we could never know any thing’s essence at any time.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00997

We can also know several truths together because one premise alone cannot produce a conclusion. If we could not know both premises at once, we could never know the conclusion. We also know both sides of a relation together, and a necessary thing together with what depends on it. These arguments show that several acts of knowledge can be present at once.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00998

This is confirmed by the soul’s experience. When the soul knows many things and reaches the level of intellect, free from the human body’s covering, it does not lose its knowledge. Rather, that knowledge becomes clearer and more open. Having moved beyond the differences of time and place, it has all its known things present at once, as with the separate intellects, whose objects of knowledge are all present together in act.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00999

You may object that when we turn our minds to understanding one thing, we cannot at that same moment turn them to understand something else. I have already pointed out that knowledge, like existence, differs in strength and weakness. Intellectual knowledge is different from imagination and sense perception. When we understand the statement “A human being is a substance, extended, growing, sensing, and rational,” the intellect grasps all these meanings together. An image corresponding to them appears in imagination. If we reverse the words—“rational, sensing, growing, extended, substance”—the meaning grasped by the intellect does not change, but the images in imagination turn around and change their order.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01000

Given this, the difficulty people find in grasping several things at once may come from the imaginative power, which has trouble presenting many different images together. These images are pictures or representations of the intellectual things the soul grasps with its intellect. The intellect itself can grasp them together. The feeling that we cannot understand many things at once may come from imagination’s difficulty in picturing them all at the same moment. Imagination can still hold together images that do not represent intelligible things. That is why it is said: the intellect makes many things one, while sense perception makes one thing many.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01001
XVII. How the Simple Soul Can Understand Many Things
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01002

We have already established that a simple thing cannot, by itself and without anything between, give rise to more than one thing. But how can one simple power give rise to many acts of understanding? An effect becomes many through one of four things: the cause itself is many; the thing receiving the effect differs; the tools differ; or the effects are arranged in a sequence. The rational soul is simple. Even if it were made of parts, their number could not match its countless acts of understanding. The many acts cannot come from many receivers either, since the receiver is the soul itself.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01003

Nor can the acts depend on one another in a sequence. Understanding black does not depend on understanding white, or white on black. The same is true of many ideas and judgments that do not make one another possible or produce one another. The remaining answer is that the tools differ. The senses, with their different organs, are like scouts bringing reports from different places. They prepare the soul to take in immaterial intellectual forms. Particular sensations multiply because the body moves in different ways to gain what is useful and avoid harm. The soul benefits from these sensations, which prepare it to form its first ideas and judgments. It then combines these, producing endlessly many further ideas and judgments. So the many first ideas arise through the different senses and tools; the ideas we learn arise as the first ones are combined in a natural order, each earlier one helping produce what comes after.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01004
XVIII. Different Ways to Classify Knowledge
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01005

As we have said many times, knowledge is immaterial existence itself. Existence is not, in itself, a general kind or species that can be divided into different types by distinguishing features, into individuals by their particular traits, or into groups by added conditions. Every act of knowledge is a simple, individual reality; it does not fall under some more basic universal kind. So when we divide knowledge, we are really dividing what is known, because knowledge and its object are one, as existence and essence are one. This is what is meant by saying that knowledge of a substance is a substance, and knowledge of a feature is a feature. Knowledge of each thing is of the same kind as the thing known.
